## In Praise of the Unfinished

I have a drawer where my former selves go to wait.

There’s a guitar with a missing tuning peg. A notebook containing four different titles for the same novel and not one chapter. Three Swedish novels with bookmarks in the early pages. A knitting project that became increasingly difficult to identify as either a sweater or a weather event.

Taken together, these objects might look like evidence of failure.

I prefer to think of them as doorways.

We are taught that finishing is a form of respect: finish the book, learn the language, play the song, complete the project. Show that you were serious. Prove that you can close the loop.

But a life is not a collection of completed tasks. Some of its best moments leave no measurable trace. Singing in the shower. Taking the long way home for no particular reason. Reading a book because a sentence feels like a window, not because you intend to remember the plot. Talking until the sky changes and discovering that you have said almost nothing about the thing you originally meant to discuss.

These experiences cannot be graded. They cannot be converted into progress. Their only achievement is having happened.

An abandoned language course does not prove that I lack discipline. It may prove that, for a while, I wanted to live inside the possibility of speaking another language. The certificate was never the point. Neither was the novel. I simply wanted to spend some evenings near them.

We are so accustomed to treating curiosity as a debt. We begin something, and immediately begin owing it an ending. A hobby becomes a performance. A private notebook becomes evidence that we are either an artist or, more likely, someone who needs a better system.

But not everything that begins needs to become a ladder. Some things are windows. Some are campsites. You can sit beside them without making a permanent home, and that does not mean the time was wasted.

There is also permission in this: you do not have to turn every interest into a career. You can make terrible pottery without becoming a ceramicist. You can dance badly without rehearsing. You can read the same nine pages for a month because those nine pages are where you feel most alive.

Tomorrow is not always a deadline. Sometimes it is just another room.

So I am keeping the unfinished guitar. I am leaving the notebook open to its fourth title. I am allowing the sweater to remain a mystery, a soft argument between wool and optimism.

Not everything needs to be completed to be loved.

Some things are still becoming. That is why we keep them.

**In Praise of the Unfinished**

I have a drawer where my former selves go to wait. A guitar ... Swiss army knife ... notebook with first line of novel ... no more than title. Little machines for postponing judgment.

We are taught a finished thing proves we tried, discipline, can close loops. But a life is not a pile of completed projects. Most valuable experiences resist evidence: walk before music, conversation with no point, swimming at night, book read for texture rather than plot. Unfinished sketch is not failed painting; gives tomorrow an entrance. Melody unfinished more vulnerable, music can knock. We keep treating curiosity like a debt.

As though evidence of failure and evidence of living not same. We can be gentle with unfinished, wonder how many lives we can love before making them efficient.

Leave sketch unfinished. Put book down with spine cracked. Let melody not know ending. Say "I don't know what I'm doing" without turning it into confession of inadequacy. Sometimes it is simply accurate, and roomy.

End: "The best things in my life haven't been completed. They've been inhabited." Maybe cliché but good. "They are still opening." More strong: "Tomorrow is not a deadline. It is another room, and I am allowed to enter without having solved the entire house." Overwrought.

"Keep one project deliberately unfinished. Not as an excuse to avoid difficulty, but as a small vote against the idea that you must earn your own attention." Nice. "Some afternoons, nothing should be finished. Some afternoons, the only task is to keep the light on." Slight sentimental.

Maybe the essay should be creative "I have a drawer where my former selves go to wait" sounds life as former selves, guilt but nuanced. 450 words. Enough. Could deliver 600.

No need cite. Final in prose.
